introduction-breaking-down-silos.core: InnerSource applies open-source practices (visible code, outside contributions, transparent review) inside a company, so teams reuse and improve each other's work instead of duplicating it.

first_principles.problem: Every department rebuilds the same thing behind walls, while the team that owns the shared component becomes a bottleneck.
truths: Knowledge hidden in silos is wasted.
Teams that need a change are motivated to make it.

analogy.title: Unlocking the filing cabinets
analogy.story: Legal's contract template, once in a shared library, stops being reinvented by Sales.
analogy.breaks: Openness alone isn't enough. Without governance and incentives, nobody contributes.

example.title: A team blocked on a platform change

check.q: What core problem does InnerSource solve?
check.a: Duplication and bottlenecks caused by siloed, closed code ownership.

governance-the-rules-of-engagement.core: InnerSource needs explicit rules: README, CONTRIBUTING.md, CODEOWNERS, review standards and response-time expectations. Openness without governance is chaos.

first_principles.problem: Letting anyone merge anything quickly degrades a shared codebase.
truths: Contributors need to know the rules up front.
derivation: **README**: what it is and how to use it.
**SLAs**: how quickly PRs get a response.

analogy.title: Community garden rules
analogy.story: Anyone can plant, but there are posted rules, plot owners and a schedule for reviewing new plantings.
analogy.breaks: Too much process scares contributors away, so keep the rules light but explicit.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Contributors know the path and reviewers are auto-assigned.

code.text:
README.md         # purpose, usage
CONTRIBUTING.md   # issue first, tests required, style
CODEOWNERS        # /src/auth @platform-auth
.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md

check.a: It automatically assigns responsible reviewers based on the paths a PR changes.

incentives-why-should-i-help-you.core: People contribute when it helps their own goals and when the organisation rewards it. Unblocking their own feature, recognition and contributions counted in performance reviews make InnerSource sustainable.

first_principles.problem: Developers measured only on their own team's features have no reason to spend days fixing another team's library.
truths: People respond to how they are measured.
derivation: Frame contributions as **unblocking your own work**.

analogy.title: Neighbourhood road repair
analogy.story: If the pothole is on your commute, you'll help fix it, especially if the council thanks you.
mapping: A blocker in a shared library
analogy.breaks: Incentives tied only to the number of PRs can be gamed with trivial changes.

example.title: A blocked feature
flow: Team B needs feature X in a shared lib

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: The incentives line up when contributing is faster than waiting.

example.outcome: contributions happen because they make sense.

check.q: Why does InnerSource fail without incentives?
check.a: People prioritise what they are measured on, so contributions to other teams' code never get time.

discoverability-finding-what-already-exi.core: Code that can't be found can't be reused. Discoverability needs a searchable catalogue (Backstage), good README metadata, code search and announcements.

first_principles.problem: A company ends up with seven rate-limiting libraries because nobody knew the first one existed.
truths: People don't search where they don't expect to find anything.

analogy.title: A library catalogue
analogy.story: Without a catalogue, books are on the shelves but no-one finds them.
analogy.breaks: A catalogue full of stale entries erodes trust, so ownership must include upkeep.

check.q: What tool is commonly used as an InnerSource service catalogue?

the-maintenance-tax-innersource-is-not-f.core: InnerSource shifts work rather than removing it. Maintainers spend real time reviewing, mentoring and owning code that others contributed, and that time must be budgeted.

first_principles.problem: Leadership expects other teams to improve the code 'for free', and the maintainers burn out under review load.
truths: Merged code has to be maintained afterwards.
derivation: Track load and **scale with trusted committers**.

analogy.title: Accepting donated furniture
analogy.story: Free furniture still needs space, cleaning and repair, and someone has to do that.
analogy.breaks: The tax still beats duplication, as long as it's planned.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Plan for the tax, or the project stalls.

check.a: Accepting contributions creates review, mentoring and long-term maintenance work for the host team.

the-trusted-committer-pattern.core: Trusted committers are experienced contributors from other teams who are given review and merge rights. They scale a popular project beyond its original maintainers and mentor newcomers.

first_principles.problem: Two maintainers with fifteen contributing teams become a bottleneck, and PRs wait for weeks.
truths: Trust can be earned and delegated.
derivation: **Grant** review and merge rights for areas they know.

analogy.title: Senior volunteers at a food bank
analogy.story: Experienced volunteers train newcomers and approve donations, so staff aren't the only gate.
analogy.breaks: Granting rights without shared standards brings inconsistency, so pair the role with guidelines.

example.title: Scaling the auth library
example.outcome: the project scales with its community.

check.q: What bottleneck does the trusted committer pattern address?
check.a: Limited review and merge capacity of the original maintainers.
